Simone, before the risk committee on Thursday, here is what you are presenting and what the room will do with it. There are three open items on the legal register. The first is the property files inside the Campinas target. The likelihood is high, because nobody has looked at them since two thousand and nineteen, but the impact is moderate, so it sits in the middle of the matrix. The second one is the reverse, and it is the one that worries me. The likelihood is low, but if it happens the severity is very high, and our exposure would be the whole value of the transaction. That is above the board threshold, which means you are required to escalate it, and the committee is going to ask you for a contingency plan, not for an opinion. The third item is already in remediation, and you can present it in one line. Two warnings on language. Do not say a risk will happen. Say it may, or it is likely to, and give the committee the number that sits behind the word. And do not tell them what the company should accept. Risk appetite is their decision, not ours. We measure it, they take it.

It is Wednesday night and I am rehearsing three minutes for the risk committee. Item one, the property files. The likelihood is high and the impact is moderate, so it sits in the middle of the matrix and I am going to mitigate it inside the department, with a date and an owner against the remediation. Item two is the one I have to get right. The likelihood is low, and I am not going to hide that, but the severity is very high and the exposure is the whole value of the transaction, which puts it above the threshold. So I escalate, and I bring a contingency plan rather than an opinion. What I have been practising is the language, because in Portuguese I say things are certain when they are not. Tonight I am striking the word will out of my notes. If it is a real possibility with numbers behind it, I say it is likely to happen. If it is a genuine maybe, I say it may happen, or it might. And if it is remote but serious, I say it could happen, which is exactly the case for item two. One last thing I keep telling myself. Nobody in that room is asking me what the company should be willing to lose. Risk appetite is theirs. My job is two honest numbers and the right modal verb in front of them.

First, you identify the risk and write it on the register in one sentence, in plain language. Then, you score it twice: how probable it is, which is the likelihood, and how much damage it would cause, which is the impact. After that, you place it on the matrix and compare it with the threshold the board has set. Next, if the score sits above that threshold, you escalate it to the committee with a contingency plan, and if it sits below, you mitigate it inside the department. Finally, you record the remediation, with a date and an owner, and you review the exposure again at the end of the quarter.
